content: When selecting antibiotics and antiseptics for maternal care, several factors must be considered, including drug tolerance, the simplest effective dose, cost-effectiveness, the most likely bacterial agents causing infection, and local susceptibility patterns in both hospital and community settings. It is essential to obtain bacterial culture samples before initiating antibiotic therapy, but this should not delay the prompt administration of antibiotics. The choice of antiseptics and antibiotics should be tailored to the maternal condition, aiming to minimize adverse effects. Ideally, antimicrobial use should be guided by local or national resistance surveillance data and treatment guidelines. The WHO recommends using alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate for skin preparation before elective or emergency cesarean sections. The method of application should follow the product’s instructions, as well as the clinician’s experience and preferences. While no specific concentration of chlorhexidine gluconate is universally recommended, most studies have used a 2% solution in 70% alcohol. It is critical to rule out maternal allergies to alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate before surgery. Even in the absence of a known allergy, clinicians should be aware that chlorhexidine gluconate can cause skin irritation. A standard preoperative skin preparation technique appropriate for the intended incision site must be followed. Drapes should not be saturated with alcohol, and pooling of the solution under the patient must be avoided. Special precautions are necessary during emergency cesarean sections. If chlorhexidine gluconate is unavailable, povidone-iodine may be used as an alternative, though it is less effective. The WHO’s current recommendations align with its 2016 global guidelines on preventing surgical site infections, which also endorse alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate for surgical skin preparation. These recommendations replace the conditional recommendation from 2015, which was based on low-quality evidence. They will also be made available on the WHO website and translated into multiple languages. National and subnational groups may adapt these recommendations to local contexts, revising existing guidelines or protocols as needed. Successful implementation requires participatory, consensus-driven processes and may involve behavior changes among healthcare practitioners to adopt evidence-based practices. In lowand middle-income countries, the availability of alcohol-based antiseptics may be limited due to financial constraints or supply chain issues. Local production of these solutions, with adequate quality control, could be a feasible and cost-effective option. Women should be adequately counseled and involved in shared decision-making regarding the use of antiseptics for skin preparation, including potential side effects. The WHO emphasizes the importance of monitoring and evaluating the implementation of these recommendations at local, national, and regional levels. Indicators such as the proportion of women receiving alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate for skin preparation and the incidence of peripartum infections after cesarean sections should be tracked. These data can inform the quality of care and the effectiveness of the intervention. The WHO will review and update these recommendations as new evidence becomes available. Stakeholders are encouraged to communicate any concerns about the validity of the recommendations and suggest additional questions for future updates.
